newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany leads drive to give stability pact teeth.
newsitem.headline: Germany leads drive to give stability pact teeth.

text.p: Germany, the bastion of stability policies, has convinced Europe of the urgent need for a pact to ensure public budgets are kept in check once a single currency is launched in 1999.

Its concern now is to make sure that the framework deal thrashed out at last weekend's meeting of European finance ministers in Dublin is fleshed out with clear definitions and penalties which give the pact real deterrent value.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, the architect of the original plans for a stability pact on fiscal issues, said he was satisfied with the meeting's outcome and added on Monday that he saw no major problems gaining agreement on the details.
"With a bit of good will, I see no more insurmountable problems," Waigel said in response to a question at a political party meeting in Munich.

Europe's ministers and central bank governors agreed in Dublin that countries participating in monetary union must keep their budget deficits below three percent of total economic output or face sanctions.
If they then failed to address the problem, the "sanction" funds deposited in a European account would be converted into a fine and transferred to EU budgets, the officials agreed.

The German delegation's insistence that it was pleased with the results of the Dublin talks seemed to many observers there nonetheless to mask some irritation that progress in nailing down the pact had not been quicker.
The finer points of the plan -- which will be crucial to its effectiveness -- were simply referred to working committees ordered to seek a consensus in the next few months.

The questions of the size of the sanctions or fines and of precise definitions for "exceptional and temporary" circumstances which would allow a country to acceptably exceed the specified deficit limit were left open.

While this weekend's agreement on the basics convinced financial markets on Monday that Europe is serious in its EMU intentions, economists say tough sanctions will be essential in harnessing market credibility for the Euro.
"The sanctions have to be such that they are visible," said Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.
"It has to be a sizeable amount of money. The pact will not present a credible threat if the sanctions or fines are a small amount of money which a government could do without."

Germany, which has presented by far the most hardline conditions for the way it believes the pact should operate, will now have to try to push these through in discussions of European experts in the build-up to a December summit meeting.
But it has found strong opposition for some of its ideas.
On the size of sanctions and fines, a German proposal calling for a deposit of 0.25 percent of GDP for each percentage point of excessive deficit is still on the table.
But it may lose out to a European Commission proposal for a a more lenient deposit of 0.1 or 0.2 percent of GDP per percentage point of excess, capped at a maximum of 0.5 percent.

EU sources also say many believe Waigel's proposal that a country should be considered in the exceptional circumstance of heavy recession only after its economy had shrunk by two percent or more is unacceptably strict.

Some argue that it is even an error to try to decide in advance what the "exceptional circumstances" may include -- which the Germans view as essential if the pact is to have any sort of fast "semi-automatic application".
"Exceptional means precisely that it could not be defined in advance," one EU source said.
But Mayer also believed it was important to establish a clear definition in advance.
"An exceptional circumsance must be in excess of a normal small recession, which ought to be covered by the normal fluctuation in deficits," he said.
